passages.happening:
“Now when the queen of Sheba heard about the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with difficult questions” (verse 1). She arrives in Jerusalem with a great caravan of camels carrying spices, gold and precious stones, and tells Solomon all that is on her mind. “And Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too difficult for the king to explain” (verse 3).

She sees his wisdom, his palace, the food at his table, the order of his servants and the offerings at the house of the LORD, and ‘it took her breath away’ (verse 5). “The report I heard in my own country about your words and wisdom is true” (verse 6), she says. “But I did not believe these things until I came and saw with my own eyes. Indeed, not even half was told to me” (verse 7). She praises the LORD, who set Solomon on the throne of Israel, and says that because of the LORD's eternal love for Israel, ‘He has made you king to carry out justice and righteousness’ (verse 9).

She gives the king a hundred and twenty talents of gold, spices and precious stones (verse 10). Hiram's fleet brings almug wood from Ophir, and Solomon makes it into steps for the temple and the palace, and into lyres and harps for the singers (verses 11-12). Solomon gives the queen all she desires, and she goes home (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Sheba, or Saba, was a kingdom in southwestern Arabia, in the region of modern Yemen. Its wealth came from frankincense, myrrh and other spices, carried north by caravan to Egypt, the Levant and Mesopotamia. Inscriptions from Saba itself come mostly from later centuries, and no text outside the Bible names this queen, so who she was cannot be checked. Arabian queens are known from Assyrian records of the eighth century BC, and a visit to a king who held the northern end of the trade routes makes good commercial sense. Later traditions told many stories of her, among them the Ethiopian royal tradition that traces its line to her and Solomon, but those stories are not in the text.

Testing a ruler with riddles and hard questions was a known contest in ancient courts, a way to measure a king's wisdom and so his worth as a partner. The word for her hard questions, chidah, also means a riddle. Her gifts and Solomon's return gifts were the formal exchange of diplomacy, and trade agreements probably lay underneath the visit.

The story is built on seeing and hearing. She hears, she sees, she says the report was true, and she did not believe until she saw. Her speech is the center of the chapter, and it praises not Solomon but the LORD. In her words the purpose of kingship is justice and righteousness, and the rest of the chapter tests Solomon against it.

The scene answers Solomon's prayer in a small way. He had asked God to hear the foreigner who comes from a distant land because of his name (8:41-43). Here one has come.
passages.later:
Jesus spoke of her: “The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31).

A psalm headed ‘Of Solomon’ hopes for the same: ‘may the kings of Sheba and Seba offer gifts’ (Psalm 72:10). The same word for a riddle is used by Samson: “Let me tell you a riddle” (Judges 14:12).
passages.asks: The queen came a long way to test what she had heard, and she went home having praised the LORD. Ask what questions you would bring to God if you came as honestly as she did. And ask what someone would see of God's goodness if they looked closely at your life.

passages.t: Gold, an ivory throne, and horses from Egypt
passages.happening:
“The weight of gold that came to Solomon each year was 666 talents” (verse 14), besides what came from merchants, traders and the kings of Arabia. He makes two hundred large shields and three hundred small shields of hammered gold and puts them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon (verses 16-17). He makes a great ivory throne overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lions standing on them. “Nothing like this had ever been made for any kingdom” (verse 20). His cups are gold, and ‘There was no silver, because it was accounted as nothing in the days of Solomon’ (verse 21). Every three years his ships of Tarshish come home with gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks (verse 22).

“So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom” (verse 23). The whole world seeks him out to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart, and every visitor brings tribute (verses 24-25).

‘Solomon accumulated 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses’ (verse 26). He makes silver as common in Jerusalem as stones (verse 27). His horses are brought from Egypt and Kue, and his merchants sell chariots and horses on to the kings of the Hittites and of Aram (verses 28-29).
passages.hearers:
The weights are enormous. A talent was roughly thirty kilograms, so 666 talents a year would be about twenty tons of gold. The throne with its six steps and lions used royal lion imagery common across the ancient Near East, and the twelve lions may echo the twelve tribes. Some of the goods are hard to identify: almug wood is unknown, and the word translated peacocks is uncertain; some translate it baboons. Ships of Tarshish probably names a class of large seagoing ship, and where Tarshish was is debated; Tartessos in Spain is the most common suggestion.

Kue is usually identified with Cilicia in the south-east of what is now Turkey, a region known for horses, and the Hittites and Aram here are the small kingdoms of Syria. The picture is of Solomon as a middleman in the trade in horses and chariots between Egypt and the north.

The list is full of superlatives: nothing like it ever made, silver counted as nothing, Solomon greater than all the kings of the earth. Read beside the law for kings in Deuteronomy, which forbids a king to gather many horses, to send the people back to Egypt for them, to take many wives, or to pile up silver and gold, the list becomes a quiet charge sheet. The chapter admires and warns in the same breath.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy's law for kings says, “But the king must not acquire many horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to acquire more horses” (Deuteronomy 17:16), and ‘He must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold’ (Deuteronomy 17:17).

Some readers also connect Solomon's 666 talents with the number in Revelation 13:18, though nothing in either text requires the link.
passages.hard:
Is this chapter praising Solomon's wealth, and is it believable?

Two questions are tangled here. On the first, interpreters differ in emphasis. Some read the chapter as a plain celebration of God's promise of riches and honor (3:13) coming true. Others note that its details, gold heaped up, horses from Egypt, and in the next chapter many wives, match item by item what Deuteronomy forbids a king, and they read the praise as deliberately double-edged. Both readings take the text seriously, and the second explains why chapter 11 follows so abruptly.

On the second, some historians regard the figures as exaggerated court language, pointing to the modest size of Jerusalem in the tenth century BC as it appears in current excavations. Others reply that ancient royal inscriptions report comparable quantities of gold, that Jerusalem's remains from that century are hard to reach beneath later cities, and that a king who taxed a trade corridor could grow rich quickly. What the chapter says about God and kingship does not depend on settling the exact weight.
passages.asks: Solomon had more than any king on earth, and the list reads like a warning. Ask what you are gathering that the law of God would ask you to hold more loosely. And ask whether your success is drawing you toward God, or back toward Egypt.
